class-struggle: In Marx's account, history is driven by conflict between social classes with opposed economic interests. Under capitalism, the owners of capital (the bourgeoisie) and those who must sell their labor to survive (the proletariat) are locked in struggle over wages, working conditions, and control of production. Many later thinkers extended the idea beyond factory and mine to conflicts over race, gender, and empire.
culture-industry: A thesis from the Frankfurt School philosophers Adorno and Horkheimer: mass-produced entertainment — film, radio, popular music — is manufactured like any other commodity, standardized to formulas. On this view, the culture industry appears to offer fun and choice while actually conditioning audiences to accept the society they live in, blunting critical thought. Critics argue it underestimates audiences' ability to resist.
epistemological-anarchism: Philosopher of science Paul Feyerabend argued there is no single scientific method — no fixed, universal rules that all good inquiry must follow. His slogan 'anything goes' meant that science has advanced by breaking rules, and that imposing one methodology would strangle discovery and suppress alternative traditions. It was a provocative plea for pluralism, not an endorsement of believing anything at all.
falsification: Karl Popper's answer to 'what makes a theory scientific?': a scientific claim must be falsifiable — it must rule something out, risking a precise prediction that observation could refute. Confirmation alone proves nothing, since endless supporting evidence can be found for vague claims like astrology. At best, a theory survives severe testing; it is never finally proven, only not yet refuted.
hegel-dialectic: Hegel's view that thought and history develop through contradiction: a position generates its own opposition, and the conflict is resolved in a richer standpoint that preserves what is true in both sides. This movement is often summarized as thesis, antithesis, synthesis — a formula Hegel himself seldom used. For Hegel, each such cycle advances humanity's self-understanding and freedom.
hegemony: Antonio Gramsci's term for rule by consent rather than force alone. A dominant class keeps power by shaping everyday culture — education, religion, media, common sense — so that its own values come to seem natural and inevitable, and the existing order appears to serve everyone. Because that consent must be continually won, it can also be contested by rival movements.
kant-phenomena-noumena: Kant's distinction between how things appear to us and how they are in themselves. Phenomena are objects as we experience them, shaped by the mind's built-in forms such as space, time, and causality. Noumena are things as they are independently of that structuring — and Kant held that human knowledge reaches only phenomena; the noumenal 'thing in itself' lies beyond experience.
male-gaze: A term from feminist film critic Laura Mulvey: mainstream visual media is conventionally shot from a male point of view, presenting women as images to be looked at and enjoyed, while men are the active lookers and heroes — and viewers are thereby positioned to adopt that perspective. The idea is widely influential and much debated, extended to advertising, literature, and games.
marx-alienation: In Marx's early writings, alienation describes how wage labor estranges workers. They lose connection with the products they make (which belong to someone else), with the activity of work itself (which becomes joyless toil), with their distinctly human capacity for free, creative production, and with one another. Work that should express who we are becomes something imposed and deforming.
master-slave-morality: Nietzsche's genealogy of Western morals: two opposing value systems. 'Master' morality calls good whatever the strong affirm — pride, excellence, nobility. 'Slave' morality, born of the powerless' repressed resentment, inverts this: meekness, humility, and pity become good while the strong are branded 'evil.' Nietzsche held that slave morality won in the West, a verdict he offered as a challenge, not praise.
objectification: Treating a person as a thing: an object to be used, a tool, a commodity, or a mere collection of parts, rather than someone with their own thoughts, feelings, and ends. Feminist philosophers have examined how pornography, advertising, and everyday life can objectify women. Many hold, with Kant, that the wrong lies in denying someone the status of an end in themselves.
paradox-of-fiction: We can be moved to tears by characters we know do not exist — yet philosophers like Colin Radford argued this is paradoxical. We seem to feel genuine emotions only about things we believe real, we know fictional characters are not real, and still we grieve for Anna Karenina. The puzzle challenges what beliefs our emotions actually require.
philosophy-of-love: From Plato to the present, philosophers have asked what love is and whether it can be justified. Is love desire for beauty, longing for union with another, or steady concern for their flourishing? And why love this particular person rather than anyone with the same qualities? The ancient Greeks distinguished eros (passionate desire), philia (friendship), and agape (selfless care) — distinctions still in use.
plato-ring-of-gyges: In Plato's Republic, Glaucon tells of a shepherd who finds a ring granting invisibility and promptly seduces the queen and murders the king. Glaucon's challenge: anyone with such a ring would act unjustly, since people behave well only to keep a reputation. The rest of the dialogue tries to show that justice is worth choosing for its own sake.
plato-tripartite-soul: In Plato's Republic the soul has three parts: reason, which calculates; spirit, the seat of honor and emotion; and appetite, which craves food, sex, money, and the like. A person is just, on Plato's view, when reason rules, spirit backs it up, and each part does its own work — mirroring his ideal city of philosophers, soldiers, and producers.
pragmatism: An American tradition founded by Charles Peirce, William James, and John Dewey. Its core idea: the meaning and worth of a belief lie in its practical consequences — what difference it would make to our actions and experience. Ideas are tools for coping with problems; inquiry is fallible and provisional, and on this view beliefs are judged by how well they work.
ressentiment: Nietzsche's term for the repressed resentment of the powerless toward those stronger than they are. Unable to act on their hatred, the weak instead perform a moral reversal: the strength of their oppressors becomes 'evil,' while their own weakness — humility, patience, meekness — is renamed 'good.' Ressentiment thus creates values, but Nietzsche thought it does so out of poison rather than strength.
scientific-realism: Should we read our best scientific theories as true descriptions of reality, including things no one can observe, like electrons and quasars? Realists say the stunning success of science would be a miracle unless theories were roughly true. Anti-realists reply that past successful theories turned out false, and the same evidence often supports rival pictures of what exists. The debate remains open.
simulacra: Jean Baudrillard's theory that in a media-saturated world, signs and images stop referring to any original reality and instead generate their own 'hyperreality.' A simulacrum is a copy without an original: the theme park, the televised event, the map that precedes the territory. On this view, what we take for the real is itself produced by simulation — a radical claim many contest.
terrorism-violence: Can violence, especially against innocents, ever be justified for political ends? Political philosophers distinguish war between armies from terrorism: the deliberate harming of randomly selected civilians to terrify a population into change. Michael Walzer argued terrorism is never justified, since innocent people may not be used as means. Others press the question of when, if ever, oppressed peoples may take up violence.
thrownness: Heidegger's term (Geworfenheit) for a basic feature of human existence: we find ourselves already 'thrown' into a life we never chose — a particular body, era, language, family, and situation — with no advance explanation of what to make of it. We can take hold of our circumstances, but never from outside them; thrownness is the unchosen starting point of every choice.
ubermensch: Nietzsche's figure of the 'overhuman' — an ideal of a person who creates their own values after the death of God, affirms life completely, including its suffering, and rises above herd morality. It is not a biological superman or a tyrant; Nietzsche gave few details. The idea has been interpreted — and exploited — in wildly different ways ever since.
utilitarianism: The view that the right action is the one that produces the most overall wellbeing (happiness, pleasure, or preference satisfaction) for everyone affected, counting each person equally. Associated with Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill, it makes consequences everything. Critics object that it can permit sacrificing an individual for the majority's sake; rule-based and other refinements respond.
will-to-power: Nietzsche's proposal that the fundamental drive in all living things is not mere survival (as Darwin held) but expansion, overcoming, and the enhancement of power — the striving to grow, shape, and master, including mastering oneself. He meant it partly as psychology, partly as a claim about life and even the world itself; scholars still dispute how far he intended it.
